Empirical Research Plan

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Stock-market event study combined with cross-sectional Difference-in-Differences (DID).  
Why this is appropriate:  
• The shocks to Continental Illinois (CI) were precise, well-publicised calendar events whose timing was exogenous to the borrowing firms.  
• Stock prices incorporate all publicly available information quickly, so abnormal returns around those dates trace the present-value effect of a sudden deterioration (or restoration) in the value of the lending relationship.  
• By comparing the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) of exposed firms with a matched, non-exposed control set we difference out economy–wide or industry-wide movements that are unrelated to CI’s problems.  
• The event-study window (e.g., –1,+1 trading days) delivers a “sharp” treatment; the DID estimator delivers the counterfactual.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
TREAT_i = 1 if firm i is documented to have a lending relationship with CI as of year-end 1983; 0 otherwise. We will also create an intensity measure:  
INTENSITY_i = (credit facility size with CI) / (market value of equity_i 12/31/83).  

Sub-groups for heterogeneous-effects tests:  
• Direct/lead borrowers (Lead_i = 1)  
• Participant-only borrowers (Lead_i = 0)  

Control group  
For every treated firm we form a matched control set (1-to-3 nearest neighbours without CI exposure) on:  
– 2-digit SIC industry  
– log(Market value of equity)  
– Book leverage (total debt / assets)  
– Ex-ante credit rating (if available)  
• Matching is done with replacement; firms that ever appear in the treated sample are discarded from the donor pool.

Treatment timing / event dates  
Negative‐news events (impairment):  
E1: 7 Mar 1984 – Sale of credit-card portfolio  
E2: 17 Apr 1984 – Discount-window borrowing disclosed  
E3: 10 May 1984 – $2 bn 28-bank lifeline announced  
E4: 17 May 1984 – Bass family withdraws as bidder  

Positive-news event (restoration):  
E5: 23 Jul 1984 – FDIC takeover announced  

For each event we compute abnormal returns in the [–1,0,+1] window. We will also check [–5,+5]. DID is implemented at the event-firm level:  

CAR_ij = α + β TREAT_i × POST_j + γ POST_j + δ TREAT_i + ε_ij  

where POST_j = 1 during the event window and 0 during an estimation window (e.g., –60 to –10).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Exogeneity of event timing: The specific calendar dates of CI distress/rescue are orthogonal to fundamentals of any individual borrower. Plausible: CI‐specific, regulator-driven events.  
A2. No differential pre-trends: In the absence of the CI shock, treated and matched controls would have followed parallel stock-return processes. Plausible if matching is successful; can be tested in pre-event windows.  
A3. Efficient markets: Prices fully and quickly reflect new information. This is the standard event-study assumption; large NYSE/AMEX firms make this reasonable.  
A4. No confounding firm-specific news in the (–1,+1) window. Partially testable by scanning news wires; we will censor observations with confounding announcements.  
A5. Stable treatment: Lending relationships did not change materially between January-1984 and the July event. Reasonable given loan contracts are typically multi-year.

4. Threats to Identification and Remedies  
T1. Selection bias: Borrowers may be systematically different from non-borrowers. Remedy: Propensity-score or exact matching on observables; include firm fixed effects when pooling multiple events.  
T2. Concurrent macro/industry shocks: Broader banking turmoil could move all corporate stock prices. Remedy: DID structure plus inclusion of daily industry returns as an additional control; placebo tests on other large-bank events where sample firms have no exposure.  
T3. Information leakage / anticipation: Markets could have partially priced CI distress prior to the chosen dates. Remedy: Inspect longer pre-event returns; include multiple earlier dates; use cumulative series of events to capture gradual information flow.

5. R Code Outline
```r
# install.packages(c("tidyverse","fixest","MatchIt","EventStudy"))
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(MatchIt)
library(EventStudy)  # any event-study or own functions

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
returns  <- read_csv("daily_returns.csv")   # columns: permno, date, ret
links    <- read_csv("ci_links.csv")        # firm_id, permno, treat, lead, facility_usd
firminfo <- read_csv("firm_characteristics.csv") # size, leverage, sic2

# 2. Build treatment indicators --------------------------------------------
links <- links %>% 
  mutate(intensity = facility_usd / size_1983)

# 3. Construct matched control sample --------------------------------------
match_data <- links %>% 
  full_join(firminfo, by = "firm_id") %>% 
  mutate(treat = if_else(is.na(treat),0,treat))

m.out <- matchit(treat ~ log(size_1983) + leverage + sic2, 
                 data = match_data, method = "nearest", ratio = 3)
matched <- match.data(m.out)

# 4. Prepare event windows --------------------------------------------------
event_dates <- tibble(event = c("E1","E2","E3","E4","E5"),
                      date  = as.Date(c("1984-03-07","1984-04-17",
                                        "1984-05-10","1984-05-17",
                                        "1984-07-23")))

# helper function to get CARs
get_car <- function(df, event_day){
  window <- df %>% 
    filter(date >= event_day-1 & date <= event_day+1) %>% 
    summarise(car = sum(ret - market_ret))  # market model with EW index
  return(window$car)
}

# Apply to each firm–event --------------------------------------------------
car_panel <- returns %>% 
  left_join(links, by = "permno") %>% 
  left_join(event_dates, by = character()) %>%       # Cartesian join
  group_by(permno, event, date_event = date.y) %>% 
  summarise(CAR = get_car(cur_data_all(), date_event),
            treat = first(treat),
            intensity = first(intensity),
            lead = first(lead),
            .groups = "drop")

# 5. Main DID regression ----------------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(CAR ~ treat*post | event + permno, 
                  data = car_panel %>% 
                          mutate(post = 1))          # only event window observations
summary(did_main)

# 6. Robustness: intensity specification -----------------------------------
did_int <- feols(CAR ~ intensity | event, data = filter(car_panel, !is.na(intensity)))
summary(did_int)

# Placebo: 100 random “pseudo events” in 1983 ------------------------------
set.seed(42)
pseudo_dates <- sample(seq(as.Date("1983-01-03"), as.Date("1983-12-30"), by="day"), 100)
# Repeat CAR calculation; verify β ≈ 0
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory predicts that borrowers lose when their relationship bank’s durability is questioned because they face higher expected future financing costs and potential search/friction costs, and gain when durability is restored. Hence:  
• CAR around E1–E4 (impairment) should be negative. I expect –1% to –3% in the 3-day window for direct/lead borrowers, roughly –0.5% for participant-only borrowers.  
• CAR around E5 (FDIC rescue) should be positive of similar magnitude but opposite sign.  
Aggregated over all impairment events, the cumulative loss might be on the order of –4% of market value for the median direct borrower.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-Study)  
C1: Event exogeneity and accurate dating – 1  
C2: No overlapping firm-specific news in window – 0.5 (we can screen but not guarantee)  
C3: Parallel return process pre-event – 1 (testable and likely)  
C4: Correct specification of market model – 1  
C5: No selection into treatment at event date – 1  
Total: 4.5 / 5

This plan delivers a transparent, testable estimate of whether and how borrowers internalise their bank’s fragility in firm value.
